items.stem: A company runs a workload on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The instance boots from a separate root volume, and the workload keeps its data on one 2 TiB Amazon EBS data volume. The workload is a relational database with small, random reads and writes that needs about 10,000 IOPS. The company must choose the volume type for the data volume. Which volume type is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?
keywords: relational database with small, random reads and writes

options.text: A General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume, with IOPS and throughput provisioned above the included baseline only as far as the workload needs them.
options.why: A database with random I/O needs SSD, and gp3 gives a [balance between cost and performance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-gp3-suited-workloads) for [medium sized single instance databases](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-use-cases).

options.text: A Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume, with IOPS provisioned for the busiest hour of the workload and kept at that level all day.
options.why: It works, but it costs more; AWS points to io2 Block Express for [higher durability, better latency consistency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-gp3-to-io2-when) or more IOPS than gp3, and the stem asks for none of these.

options.text: A Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume, sized so that its throughput matches the reads and writes that the workload performs each day.
options.why: A transactional workload with small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), so st1 fails the 10,000 IOPS need of the database.

options.text: A Cold HDD (sc1) volume, which has the lowest storage price per GB of all EBS volume types, sized to hold the data of the workload.
options.why: The lowest price does not help when the volume fails the need: sc1 fits [colder data requiring fewer scans per day](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-sc1-use-cases), not small, random database I/O.

items.explanation: Small, random reads and writes at about 10,000 IOPS decide this question. SSD volumes serve [transactional, IOPS-intensive database workloads, boot volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-ssd-workloads), and HDD volumes do not. Among the SSD types, gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd), and you provision its IOPS [independently of volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), so the database gets its IOPS without the price of io2 Block Express.
items.takeaway: Small, random database I/O at a moderate IOPS level points to gp3, the lowest-cost SSD type.
items.twin: If the stem said "a log processing job that reads large files sequentially many times a day and must finish each scan quickly" instead: st1, which fits [big data, data warehouses, log processing](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-st1-use-cases).
items.say: It's a database with random I/O at a normal IOPS level, so I'd pick gp3.

solvers.stem_only: gp3: random small I/O at 10,000 IOPS needs SSD; gp3 includes a baseline of IOPS independent of size and lets you buy extra IOPS cheaply, so provision 10,000 IOPS on a 2 TiB gp3 volume. io2 costs more and HDD types cannot do random IOPS.

items.stem: A company runs a database on one Amazon EC2 instance that stores its data on one Amazon EBS volume. The company accepts the loss of up to one day of data and a recovery time of several hours. The company does not run any of its instances across multiple Availability Zones today. The company must be able to recover the database if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable
loss of up to one day of data

options.text: Take a daily snapshot of the volume. After a failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone of the same Region.
options.why: A snapshot outlives the zone because its data is [stored redundantly in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-stored-in-s3-multiple-azs), and a daily snapshot meets the one-day loss limit.

options.text: Take a daily snapshot of the volume and copy it to a second Region. After a failure, create a volume from the copy there.
options.why: It works, but a copy is [charged for the data transferred across regions](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-charge) and stored twice, and the loss of one zone does not need a second Region.

options.text: Keep the data on the current volume. After a failure, detach the volume and attach it to a new instance in another Availability Zone of the Region.
options.why: The volume and the instance [must be in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance), so the volume in the failed zone cannot be attached to an instance in another zone.

options.text: Take a daily snapshot and copy it to a second Region. Keep a standby instance running there, and restore each new copy to its volume.
options.why: It works, but a standby instance that runs every day and a copy in a second Region cost more, and the company accepts several hours of recovery.
options.misconception: a database can be recovered only from a standby instance that is already running

items.explanation: The loss of one zone, with one day of data loss allowed, decides this question. Snapshot data is [replicated across all Availability Zones in the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region), so you can [restore volumes in any Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region) of that Region after the zone fails. A daily snapshot meets the one-day limit, and the company pays for no copy in a second Region and no running standby.
items.takeaway: The loss of a zone needs a snapshot restored in another zone; the loss of a Region needs a copy in another Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "if the whole Region becomes unavailable" instead: copy each snapshot to a second Region, because [snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing) where they are created.
items.say: A daily snapshot is enough: I can restore it in any other zone of the Region.

solvers.stem_only: Daily EBS snapshots (stored regionally, not tied to one AZ); after an AZ failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another AZ of the same Region and attach it to a new instance. RPO 1 day and RTO hours fit; no cross-Region copy or standby needed.

items.stem: A company runs a media processing application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. Each instance writes many working files while it processes a job, and the job needs fast performance for small, random reads and writes. The files are temporary scratch data that the application can re-create from Amazon S3, and the storage must give the lowest latency possible. Which storage solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Launch the fleet on an instance type that provides instance store volumes, and write the working files to those volumes.
options.why: Instance store fits [buffers, caches, scratch data](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-ideal-for-temporary-data) and gives [high random I/O performance with very low latency](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-ssd-high-random-io).

options.text: Attach a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
options.why: It works, but each volume is [charged by the amount of GB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month) that you provision, and average EBS latency is [single-digit milliseconds](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-average-latency) for files that the job can re-create.

options.text: Create one Amazon EFS file system, mount it on every instance in the fleet, and write the working files to it.
options.why: Amazon EFS is for [shared read and write access across multiple Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-decision-guide-file-storage-shared-access), but each instance here works on its own scratch files.
options.misconception: chooses shared file storage for files that no other instance reads

options.text: Attach a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
options.why: Small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), so the job loses the fast reads and writes that it needs.

items.explanation: Instance store is [temporary block-level storage](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-physically-attached-host-disks) on disks of the host computer, and [there is no additional charge](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-no-additional-charge) for it. Its data is lost when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop). That loss costs nothing here, because the application can re-create the files from Amazon S3.
items.takeaway: Scratch data that can be re-created and needs the lowest latency goes on instance store, not on EBS.
items.twin: If the stem said "the files must still be there after a weekly stop and start" instead: a gp3 volume on each instance, because it [remains attached throughout the stop-start cycle](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start).

solvers.stem_only: Instance store: temporary, re-creatable scratch data with lowest latency, physically attached NVMe disks included in the instance price.

items.stem: A company launches Amazon EC2 instances from a launch template. Each instance has one Amazon EBS root volume, and the template keeps the default settings for that volume. When the company terminates an instance, the root volume disappears. An auditor now requires the company to retain the data of each root volume after its instance is terminated. What should the company change in the launch template for future launches?
keywords: retain the data of each root volume

options.text: Make no change, because Amazon EBS volumes persist after their instance is terminated, whatever the settings are.
options.why: The root volume created at launch is [deleted when that instance is terminated](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true) while its flag keeps the default.

options.text: Add an instance store volume to the template, and copy the root volume data to it before each termination.
options.why: Instance store data is lost when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop), so the copy disappears with the instance.

options.text: Set the DeleteOnTermination attribute of the root volume to true in the block device mapping of the template.
options.why: A true flag deletes the volume at termination, which is the behavior the company has now, because [the default is to delete the root volume](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-delete-on-termination-defaults).
options.misconception: reads DeleteOnTermination set to true as the setting that keeps the volume

options.text: Set the DeleteOnTermination attribute of the root volume to false in the block device mapping of the template.
options.why: The root volume stays after termination when you set [DeleteOnTermination to false](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-delete-on-termination-root-default-true) at launch.

items.explanation: Each EBS volume has a [DeleteOnTermination](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-delete-on-termination-defaults) attribute, and [the default is to delete the root volume](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-delete-on-termination-defaults) when the instance terminates. To keep a root volume, AWS says to set its [Delete on termination flag](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-root-delete-on-termination-no) to No, which is false in the block device mapping of the template.
items.takeaway: The root volume is deleted at termination unless DeleteOnTermination is false.
items.twin: If the stem said "retain a second data volume that was created at launch" instead: no change is needed, because other volumes created at launch [are not deleted when that instance is terminated](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-delete-on-termination-additional-default-false).

solvers.stem_only: Root volumes default to DeleteOnTermination = true; set DeleteOnTermination to false for the root volume in the block device mapping of the launch template.

items.stem: A company has taken a daily snapshot of an Amazon EBS data volume for the past year, and it keeps every snapshot. Snapshot storage costs are growing. The company needs to restore the volume to a point in time from any of the last 7 days, and it does not need older restore points. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: does not need older restore points

options.text: Keep every daily snapshot, because each incremental snapshot depends on the older ones and a deletion would break the newer restores.
options.why: It works, but it pays for a year of unneeded restore points; you [retain only the most recent snapshot](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-deletion-keep-only-latest) to restore the volume.

options.text: Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy with a daily schedule and age-based retention of 7 days, and delete the older snapshots.
options.why: Deleting a snapshot removes [only the data that is referenced exclusively](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-delete-removes-only-exclusive-data) by it, and the policy keeps snapshots by [either their total count or their age](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-schedule-frequency-and-retention-type).

options.text: Move every daily snapshot to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier, and restore an archived snapshot when the company needs a restore point.
options.why: AWS recommends the archive tier for [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily), and archiving daily incremental snapshots [can lead to higher costs](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily).

options.text: Keep every daily snapshot, and copy the data to a smaller new volume, because snapshot charges follow the provisioned size of the volume.
options.why: Snapshot charges are based on [the size of the data being backed up](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-charged-by-data-not-volume-size), so a smaller volume with the same data saves nothing.
options.misconception: believes that snapshot charges follow the provisioned size of the source volume

items.explanation: Snapshots are [incremental backups](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-incremental-changed-blocks), but deleting an older one [does not affect your ability to create volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-delete-removes-only-exclusive-data) from later snapshots. A Data Lifecycle Manager policy automates the [creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis), so the company keeps 7 days of restore points and pays for no older data.
items.takeaway: Deleting old snapshots keeps the newer ones restorable; a retention rule removes what you no longer need.
items.twin: If the stem said "keeps one snapshot each month for seven years and rarely reads it" instead: the archive tier, which AWS recommends for [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily).

solvers.stem_only: Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager with daily snapshots and 7-day retention, and delete older snapshots; deleting older incremental snapshots does not break newer ones because needed blocks are kept.

items.stem: A company runs a PostgreSQL database on one Amazon EC2 instance. The database uses a 2 TiB General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS data volume, but the volume holds only 200 GiB of data, and the data grows slowly. The company wants to cut the monthly storage cost of this volume. The database team accepts a short maintenance window. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Modify the existing volume to 300 GiB with Elastic Volumes while the database runs, and then shrink the partition and the file system.
options.why: Elastic Volumes can grow a volume, but [you can't decrease the volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease), so the change to a smaller size fails.

options.text: Create a snapshot of the volume, restore the snapshot into a new 300 GiB gp3 volume, switch the database to it, and delete the old volume.
options.why: A volume restored from a snapshot must be [equal to or larger than](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-from-snapshot-size-at-least-source) the snapshot's volume size, so a restore cannot make it smaller.
options.misconception: believes that a snapshot can be restored into a volume that is smaller than its source volume

options.text: Create a new 300 GiB gp3 volume, copy the data to it with a file copy tool, switch the database to it, and delete the old volume.
options.why: Because [you can't decrease the volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease), you [create a smaller volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease) and copy the data; the new size leaves room for slow growth.

options.text: Create a new 1 TiB gp3 volume, copy the data to it with a file copy tool, switch the database to it, and delete the old volume.
options.why: It works, but storage is [charged by the amount of GB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month) that you provision, and that size is far more than the slowly growing data needs.

items.explanation: Storage is [charged by the amount of GB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-billed-provisioned-gb-month) that you provision, so the cost follows the 2 TiB, not the 200 GiB of data. Elastic Volumes does not help here, because [you can't decrease the volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-size-cannot-decrease). The way down is a new, smaller volume, a copy of the data in the maintenance window, and the deletion of the old volume.
items.takeaway: An EBS volume grows in place but does not shrink; to shrink, copy the data to a smaller new volume.
items.twin: If the stem said "the volume is nearly full and the data keeps growing" instead: increase the size with Elastic Volumes, [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).
items.say: A volume does not shrink, so copy the data to a smaller new volume and delete the big one.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective way to cut the storage cost of one volume.
I mark the constraints: a 2 TiB gp3 volume, 200 GiB of slowly growing data, a database, and a short maintenance window that the team accepts.
Before I look at the options, I predict Elastic Volumes: I modify the volume to a smaller size while the database runs.

I remove the new 1 TiB volume, because it still pays for far more storage than the data needs. I remove the snapshot restore, because a volume from a snapshot is equal to or larger than the snapshot's volume size.

Between the Elastic Volumes change and the copy to a new 300 GiB volume the difference is direction. My first idea breaks because you can't decrease the volume size with Elastic Volumes; AWS says to create a smaller volume and copy the data, and the maintenance window allows that.
Check: the new 300 GiB gp3 volume holds the data with room to grow, and deleting the old volume ends its charge. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: EBS volumes cannot be shrunk with Elastic Volumes, and a volume restored from a snapshot cannot be smaller than the snapshot's source size. Create a new smaller gp3 volume (sized for data plus growth, e.g. a few hundred GiB), copy data at file level, switch over in a maintenance window, delete the old volume.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Users upload images, and every instance must read and write the same set of image files with standard file operations. The solution must keep working if one Availability Zone fails. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: every instance must read and write the same set of image files
keep working if one Availability Zone fails

options.text: Create one Amazon EFS file system, and configure every instance to mount it at startup in each Availability Zone.
options.why: Amazon EFS stores data [within and across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing) and gives [shared read and write access across multiple Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-decision-guide-file-storage-shared-access).

options.text: Create one Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume with Multi-Attach enabled, and attach the volume to every instance in each Availability Zone.
options.why: Multi-Attach works for instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), and with several writers you [use a clustered file system](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system), not standard file operations.

options.text: Attach a gp3 volume to each instance, and run a scheduled job on every instance that copies new image files to the other instances.
options.why: It works, but the team builds and runs a copy job on every instance, which is more work than one shared file system.
options.misconception: copies files between instances instead of using shared file storage

options.text: Use the instance store volumes of each instance, and run a scheduled job on every instance that copies new image files to the other instances.
options.why: Instance store data is lost when an instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop), and Auto Scaling terminates instances, so uploaded images can disappear.

items.explanation: Every instance, in several zones, reads and writes the same files, so the need is shared file storage. Amazon EFS is a [file storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object) that stores data [within and across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing). An EBS volume is [automatically replicated within its Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-replicated-within-az), so a volume belongs to one zone.
items.takeaway: Shared files across Availability Zones point to Amazon EFS; an EBS volume stays in one zone.
items.twin: If the stem said "two cluster nodes in one Availability Zone share one block device" instead: an io2 volume with Multi-Attach, which can [attach a single Provisioned IOPS SSD](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) volume to several instances.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon EFS (Regional, multi-AZ) mounted by every instance via NFS: shared file semantics across AZs with no replication jobs to manage.

items.stem: A company runs automated tests on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone. Each morning, on a predictable schedule, the company creates four Amazon EBS volumes from the same 50 GiB snapshot and attaches them to the fleet. The first test runs are slow, because the new volumes do not deliver their full performance at first. The volumes must deliver full performance from the first test run, which starts as soon as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: do not deliver their full performance at first
full performance from the first test run

options.text: Make no change to the process, because a volume that is created from a snapshot delivers its full performance as soon as it exists.
options.why: Each block is [downloaded from Amazon S3 to the new volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot) on first read, so the volume shows [increased I/O latency and decreased performance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot) at first.

options.text: Create the four volumes as Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volumes with high provisioned IOPS, so that they start at full speed.
options.why: The blocks of an io2 volume are also [downloaded from Amazon S3 to the new volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot) on first read, so more provisioned IOPS do not remove the slow start.

options.text: Write a script that creates the volumes each evening and reads every block of each volume with the dd utility before the tests.
options.why: It works, because you can [use the dd or fio utilities](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-manual-initialization-read-all-blocks) to read every block, but the team builds and runs a nightly script and pays for extra volume hours.

options.text: Enable fast snapshot restore on the snapshot in the Availability Zone of the fleet, and keep creating the volumes from that snapshot.
options.why: Volumes from a snapshot with fast snapshot restore are [fully initialized at creation](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-fsr-volume-fully-initialized-at-creation) and deliver full performance from the first test run.

items.explanation: A volume from a snapshot shows [increased I/O latency and decreased performance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot) until each block has been read once. Fast snapshot restore lets you [avoid the initial performance hit during initialization](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-fsr-when-to-use), and test and development volume copies are one of its use cases. The company enables it on one snapshot in one zone and changes nothing else.
items.takeaway: A volume restored from a snapshot starts slow; fast snapshot restore makes it fully initialized at creation.
items.twin: If the stem said "the company creates new, empty volumes each morning" instead: no change is needed, because empty volumes [do not require initialization](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-empty-volume-no-initialization).

solvers.stem_only: Enable EBS fast snapshot restore on the snapshot in the fleet's AZ so new volumes are fully initialized at creation, with no pre-warming scripts.

verification.note: claims-22-008: explanation says blocks load on first read, which no saved page supports; unshipped without an edit so the verified text is not changed; ebs-q015 ships instead

items.stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that store data on Amazon EBS volumes in one AWS Region. The company must back up the volumes every day and keep each backup for 30 days. Operators sometimes delete snapshots by mistake, and the company must be able to recover a snapshot that was deleted in the last week. The company wants to automate the solution. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: back up the volumes every day
recover a snapshot that was deleted

options.text: Rely on the replication that Amazon EBS performs for every volume, because it already keeps extra copies of the data for recovery.
options.why: Replication protects against the [failure of any single hardware component](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-replicated-within-az), not against a deleted snapshot or a lost zone.

options.text: Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that targets the volumes by tag, takes a snapshot every day, and keeps each snapshot for 30 days.
options.why: A policy automates the [creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis) and keeps them by [either their total count or their age](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-schedule-frequency-and-retention-type).

options.text: Run a cron job on each instance that calls the AWS CLI every day to create snapshots and to delete the snapshots that are older than 30 days.
options.why: It works, but the team writes and maintains a script on every instance, while a policy does the job [at no additional cost](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-automates-snapshots-and-amis).

options.text: Change the volumes to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volumes, because their higher durability removes the need for daily snapshots.
options.why: Durability, snapshots and copies in other zones [protect against different types of failures](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-io2-still-snapshot-and-replicate), so durability is no backup.

options.text: Create a Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots in the Region, with a retention period that keeps deleted snapshots for at least 7 days.
options.why: Recycle Bin protects snapshots after you create rules [in the AWS Regions in which you want](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-recycle-bin-needs-regional-retention-rules) protection, and you restore [at any time before its retention period expires](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-recycle-bin-expired-permanently-deleted).

items.explanation: AWS [does not automatically back up the data](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-no-automatic-backup-customer-creates-snapshots), so a Data Lifecycle Manager policy takes the daily snapshots and deletes them after 30 days. A deletion by mistake needs a second guard: a deleted snapshot that matches a retention rule is [retained in the Recycle Bin](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-delete-retained-by-recycle-bin-rule) and can be restored.
items.takeaway: Schedule snapshots with Data Lifecycle Manager, and undo deletions with a Recycle Bin rule in each Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "one policy must cover Amazon EBS, Amazon RDS and Amazon EFS across accounts" instead: AWS Backup, because you [apply it across accounts and Regions](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-aws-backup-central-policy-across-accounts).

solvers.stem_only: Data Lifecycle Manager (or AWS Backup) policy for daily snapshots with 30-day retention, plus a Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots that keeps deleted snapshots for at least 7 days.

items.stem: A company runs a mission-critical database on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The database makes small, random reads and writes and needs about 12,000 IOPS. It needs low latency: the storage must give consistent sub-millisecond latency. The data volume must also have the highest durability that Amazon EBS offers. Which storage configuration is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?
keywords: the highest durability that Amazon EBS offers

options.text: Use one General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume, and provision 12,000 IOPS and the throughput that the database needs above the included baseline.
options.why: gp3 gives [single-digit millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-latency) and is designed for [99.8 percent to 99.9 percent](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-durability-afr) durability, so it fails both storage requirements.
options.misconception: provisioned IOPS on gp3 also give sub-millisecond latency and the highest durability

options.text: Use one Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume that is large enough to give the database high throughput for its reads and writes.
options.why: A database with small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), and st1 fails the latency need as well.

options.text: Use two Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volumes in a RAID 1 mirror, and provision 12,000 IOPS on each volume.
options.why: It meets the needs, but two volumes double the cost, and AWS says [RAID 1 is also not recommended](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-raid1-not-recommended) for EBS volumes.
options.misconception: two mirrored io2 volumes are needed to reach the highest durability

options.text: Use one Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume, and provision the 12,000 IOPS that the database needs on that volume.
options.why: io2 Block Express gives [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases) and is designed for [99.999 percent volume durability](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-durability-afr).

items.explanation: Sub-millisecond latency and the highest EBS durability decide this question. io2 Block Express is the EBS type for [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases), and it offers [100X greater durability](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-io2-durability-99999) than other EBS volumes. One volume with the needed IOPS meets both requirements, so a mirror adds cost and meets no extra requirement.
items.takeaway: Sub-millisecond latency or the highest EBS durability points to one io2 Block Express volume.
items.twin: If the stem said "single-digit millisecond latency and normal EBS durability are acceptable" instead: one gp3 volume with provisioned IOPS, for a [balance between cost and performance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-gp3-suited-workloads).
items.say: Sub-millisecond latency and top durability on one volume means io2 Block Express.

solvers.stem_only: One io2 Block Express volume with 12,000 provisioned IOPS: io2 gives the highest EBS durability (99.999%) and sub-millisecond latency; gp3 has lower durability, and mirroring doubles the cost.

items.stem: A company stores customer data on Amazon EBS volumes and takes daily snapshots of them. All of the snapshots are encrypted with the AWS managed key for Amazon EBS. A new security rule requires a copy of each snapshot in a separate, isolated backup account in the same AWS Region, so that a compromise of the production account does not reach the copies. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?
keywords: encrypted with the AWS managed key

options.text: Share the existing snapshots with the backup account, and let the backup account copy them with a KMS key that it owns.
options.why: [You can't share snapshots that are encrypted](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-aws-managed-key-not-shareable) with the AWS managed key, so the backup account gets nothing to copy.

options.text: Edit the key policy of the AWS managed key for Amazon EBS to allow the backup account, and share the existing snapshots with that account.
options.why: You [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), including their key policies, so the backup account gets no access.

options.text: Copy the snapshots with a customer managed key, share that key and the copies with the backup account, and let that account copy them with a KMS key that it owns.
options.why: A copy can use a new key [during a snapshot copy operation](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-key-fixed-change-on-copy), and to share the copy [you must also share the customer managed key](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-share-encrypted-share-cmk-too).

options.text: Copy the snapshots with a customer managed key, share that key and the copies with every account in the organization, and let each account copy them with its own key.
options.why: It works, but every account in the organization can then read the copies, which is less secure than one isolated account.
options.misconception: sharing a backup with every account of the organization is as safe as sharing it with one account

items.explanation: The AWS managed key decides this question. Only snapshots [encrypted with a customer managed key](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-aws-managed-key-not-shareable) can be shared. So the company copies each snapshot with that kind of key and shares the key and the copies with the one backup account. That account then copies them [using a KMS key that you own](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-shared-snapshot-recopy-with-own-key), which guards against [your account being compromised](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-dlm-cross-account-copy-isolated-account).
items.takeaway: To share an encrypted snapshot, copy it with a customer managed key, share it with one account, and let that account copy again.
items.twin: If the stem said "the snapshots are encrypted with a customer managed key" instead: share the snapshots directly and give the backup account permission on that key, because [you must also share the customer managed key](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-share-encrypted-share-cmk-too).
items.say: I'd copy the snapshots with a customer managed key, share it with the backup account only, and let that account copy them again.

solvers.stem_only: Snapshots encrypted with the AWS managed key for EBS cannot be shared, and that key's policy cannot be edited. Copy each snapshot re-encrypted with a customer managed key, grant only the backup account use of that key, share the copies with only that account, and have the backup account copy them again with a KMS key it owns, so its copies no longer depend on any production-account key.

items.stem: A company runs an application on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The application writes its data to a 500 GiB gp3 Amazon EBS data volume, and the volume is almost full. The data grows by about 20 GiB each week. The application cannot be stopped, so the team must add storage without downtime. Which action should the team take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Stop the instance, detach the volume, and attach a new, larger gp3 volume that holds a copy of the data.
options.why: Stopping the instance is downtime, and Elastic Volumes grows a volume [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).

options.text: Increase the size of the volume with Elastic Volumes, and then extend the partition and the file system inside the instance.
options.why: Elastic Volumes can [increase the volume size, change the volume type](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach) in place, and after that [you must also extend the volume's partition](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-extend-partition-after-size-increase).

options.text: Create a snapshot of the volume, restore the snapshot to a larger gp3 volume, and switch the application to the restored volume.
options.why: The switch interrupts the application, and a restored volume is slow at first because its blocks are [downloaded from Amazon S3 to the new volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-initialization-from-snapshot).

options.text: Attach an instance store volume to the running instance, and move the oldest data of the application to that volume.
options.why: You can attach instance store volumes to an instance [only when you launch it](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-attach-only-at-launch), so the running instance cannot get one.
options.misconception: an instance store volume can be added to a running instance like an EBS volume

items.explanation: The words "without downtime" decide this question. With Elastic Volumes you can increase the size of a volume [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach). The new size can be used after the modification [reaches the optimizing state](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-modification-size-effective-at-optimizing), and then you extend the partition and the file system.
items.takeaway: More space with no downtime means Elastic Volumes, then a larger partition and file system.
items.twin: If the stem said "the volume has free space, but the database needs more IOPS" instead: provision more IOPS on the gp3 volume, again [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).
items.say: I'd grow the volume with Elastic Volumes and then extend the file system.

solvers.stem_only: Use Elastic Volumes to increase the gp3 volume size online, then extend the partition and file system inside the OS; no stop needed.

items.stem: A company runs an application on two Amazon EC2 Linux instances that are built on the Nitro System. Both instances are in the same Availability Zone. The application must be highly available, so both nodes must read and write the same block storage at the same time, and either node must be able to take over at once. The application itself does not coordinate writes between the two nodes. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to both instances.
options.why: Multi-Attach lets you [attach a single Provisioned IOPS SSD](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), as these two nodes are.

options.text: Create a General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to both instances in the zone.
options.why: Multi-Attach is [supported exclusively on](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-only) io1 and io2 volumes, so a gp3 volume cannot serve both instances.

options.text: Format the shared volume with the XFS file system, and mount the file system on both instances at the same time.
options.why: XFS is [not designed to be accessed simultaneously](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system) by several instances, so two nodes that mount it can corrupt the data.

options.text: Format the shared volume with a clustered file system, and let the cluster software coordinate the writes of both nodes.
options.why: With Multi-Attach you should [use a clustered file system](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system), which keeps the writes of both nodes safe.

options.text: Write new code in the application that coordinates every write of both nodes to the shared volume at the block level.
options.why: Code that [coordinates safe access at the application-level](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-multi-attach-application-requirements) can work, but it is new code to build and test.
options.misconception: the team must write its own code to coordinate writes to a shared volume

items.explanation: One zone and one shared block device decide this question. Multi-Attach gives each attached instance [full read and write permission](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az) on one io2 volume. Standard file systems are not built for that, and the application does not order its own writes, so you [use a clustered file system](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-needs-clustered-file-system) and let the cluster software order them.
items.takeaway: Shared block storage for a cluster in one zone means io2 with Multi-Attach and a clustered file system.
items.twin: If the stem said "web servers in three Availability Zones need the same files" instead: Amazon EFS, which stores data [within and across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-vs-efs-az-scope-and-sharing).
items.say: Two nodes in one zone can share one io2 volume with Multi-Attach, on a clustered file system.

solvers.stem_only: Use EBS Multi-Attach, which is available only on Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2) volumes on Nitro instances in the same AZ, and put a cluster-aware file system (for example GFS2 or OCFS2) on the volume so the cluster software coordinates concurrent writes; a standard file system such as XFS or ext4 would corrupt data, and writing custom block-level coordination is high overhead.

items.stem: A company runs a database on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The database uses two io2 Block Express data volumes with 12,000 provisioned IOPS each. The instance type supports at most 15,000 IOPS for Amazon EBS traffic. Monitoring shows that the database reaches about 15,000 IOPS in total. However, neither volume reaches its provisioned IOPS. The team must raise the I/O performance of the database. Which solution is the MOST operationally efficient way to meet this requirement?
keywords: at most 15,000 IOPS for Amazon EBS traffic
neither volume reaches its provisioned IOPS

options.text: Raise the provisioned IOPS of both io2 Block Express volumes with Elastic Volumes, so that each volume has more IOPS than the database needs.
options.why: Performance is limited by the instance or the volumes, [whichever is smaller](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller), and the instance limit is already reached.

options.text: Add a third io2 Block Express volume, and stripe the three volumes in a RAID 0 array so that their IOPS add up for the database.
options.why: RAID 0 adds the IOPS of the volumes, but the total stays [bounded by the instance type's performance limits](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller).

options.text: Move half of the data to a second instance of the same type with one of the volumes, and change the application to split its queries.
options.why: It works, but a second instance and a change to the application take far more effort than one change of instance type.
options.misconception: the only way past one instance limit is to split the database across instances

options.text: Change the instance to a larger Nitro-based instance type whose EBS limit is higher than the total provisioned IOPS of both volumes.
options.why: EBS performance is [bounded by the instance type's performance limits](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller), so a type with a higher EBS limit lets both volumes reach their provisioned IOPS.

items.explanation: The total of about 15,000 IOPS, equal to the instance limit, decides this question. An instance's EBS performance is [bounded by the instance type's performance limits](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller) or by its volumes, [whichever is smaller](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller). Here the instance is the smaller limit, so a larger Nitro-based type raises the ceiling with no change to the volumes or the application.
items.takeaway: When an instance reaches its EBS limit, a larger instance type helps, and more volume IOPS do not.
items.twin: If the stem said "the instance supports 40,000 IOPS, and each volume runs at its provisioned IOPS" instead: raise the provisioned IOPS of the volumes, because performance follows the instance or the volumes, [whichever is smaller](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-instance-performance-bounded-by-smaller).
items.say: The instance is the bottleneck, so I'd move to a larger instance type.

solvers.stem_only: The bottleneck is the instance's EBS IOPS limit (15,000), not the volumes (24,000 provisioned). Move to a larger Nitro instance type with a higher EBS IOPS limit.

items.stem: A company runs a workload on one Amazon EC2 instance that is built on the Nitro System. The instance boots from a separate root volume, and the workload keeps its data on one 2 TiB Amazon EBS data volume. The workload is a log processing job that reads large files sequentially many times a day and must finish each scan quickly. Each scan needs a sustained read throughput of 60 MiB/s from start to end. The company must choose the volume type for the data volume. Which volume type is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?
keywords: reads large files sequentially many times a day

options.text: A General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume, with IOPS and throughput provisioned above the included baseline only as far as the workload needs them.
options.why: gp3 meets the rate, but in the example Region its storage costs [$0.08 per GB-month](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-storage-price-example), against [$0.045 per GB-month](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-st1-storage-price-example) for st1.
options.misconception: SSD is the cheapest fit for any workload that must be fast

options.text: A Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) volume, with IOPS provisioned for the busiest hour of the workload and kept at that level all day.
options.why: It works, but io2 Block Express is for needs such as [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases), which a log scan does not have.
options.misconception: the fastest SSD type is needed for fast scans

options.text: A Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume, sized so that its throughput matches the reads and writes that the workload performs each day.
options.why: st1 is built for [big data, data warehouses, log processing](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-st1-use-cases), and after a burst it keeps [40 MiB/s per TiB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-st1-max-throughput), which covers 60 MiB/s on 2 TiB.

options.text: A Cold HDD (sc1) volume, which has the lowest storage price per GB of all EBS volume types, sized to hold the data of the workload.
options.why: sc1 costs less per GB, but after its burst it falls to [12 MiB/s per TiB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-sc1-max-throughput), which is well below 60 MiB/s on a 2 TiB volume.

items.explanation: A steady 60 MiB/s of large, sequential reads decides this question. HDD volumes measure performance [in terms of throughput rather than IOPS](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-hdd-performance-in-throughput-not-iops), and st1 is designed for [frequently accessed, throughput-intensive workloads](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-st1-low-cost-frequent-throughput) such as log processing. sc1 fits [colder data requiring fewer scans per day](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-sc1-use-cases), and gp3 costs more per GB than st1 for the same scan.
items.takeaway: Frequent large, sequential scans point to st1; rare scans of cold data point to sc1.
items.twin: If the stem said "a relational database with small, random reads and writes that needs about 10,000 IOPS" instead: gp3, because such a workload [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io).
items.say: Big sequential scans many times a day: that's st1.

solvers.stem_only: Large sequential reads with a sustained throughput need on a multi-TiB volume point to Throughput Optimized HDD (st1): its baseline throughput scales with size, so a 2 TiB st1 volume has a baseline above 60 MiB/s at a lower price per GB than gp3. Cold HDD (sc1) has too low a baseline to sustain 60 MiB/s across repeated scans, and SSD types cost more.

docs/ebs/latest/userguide/hdd-vols#if you have a throughput-oriented worklo

solvers.flag: D (gp3) also meets 60 MiB/s with its included baseline, so B wins only on price per GB, which the stem does not state; B's phrase 'sized so that its throughput matches the reads and writes that the workload performs each day' is also muddled (st1 throughput scales with volume size, not with daily volume), so a careful candidate could read B as a wrong sizing rule and pick D.

items.stem: A company runs a MySQL database on one Amazon EC2 instance. The database stores its data on a 100 GiB General Purpose SSD (gp2) Amazon EBS volume. After a product launch, the database needs 8,000 IOPS, but the volume does not deliver that many IOPS. The data will stay near 100 GiB for the next year. The change must cause minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Increase the size of the gp2 volume with Elastic Volumes until its baseline performance reaches 8,000 IOPS, and keep the gp2 volume type.
options.why: It works, but gp2 baseline IOPS grow at [3 IOPS per GiB](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp2-iops-per-gib), so the company pays for many times the storage that the data needs.

options.text: Attach more gp2 volumes, build a RAID 0 array across all of them, and move the database files to the array to add their IOPS.
options.why: [Creating a RAID 0 array](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-raid0-more-than-one-volume) adds the IOPS of each volume, but the extra volumes add storage, and moving the database files adds downtime.
options.misconception: stripes several gp2 volumes when one gp3 volume can provision the IOPS in place

options.text: Change the volume type to gp3 with Elastic Volumes while the database runs, and provision 8,000 IOPS on the same 100 GiB volume.
options.why: gp3 provisions IOPS [independently of volume size](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), and Elastic Volumes changes the type [without detaching the volume or restarting the instance](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-elastic-volumes-modify-without-detach).

options.text: Change the volume type to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) with Elastic Volumes while the database runs, and provision 8,000 IOPS.
options.why: It works, but AWS recommends io2 Block Express for [higher durability, better latency consistency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-gp3-to-io2-when) or more than gp3 gives, and the stem asks for neither.

items.explanation: gp3 separates size and speed: you provision IOPS [without needing to provision additional block storage capacity](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-performance-independent-of-size), so the volume stays at 100 GiB. Elastic Volumes makes the change while the database runs. gp3 is also [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd) type, so the company pays for no extra storage and no premium volume type.
items.takeaway: More IOPS without more space: change gp2 to gp3 in place and provision the IOPS.
items.twin: If the stem said "the database also needs consistent sub-millisecond latency" instead: io2 Block Express, because it serves workloads that need [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases).
items.say: Change the gp2 volume to gp3 in place and buy the IOPS you need, without paying for space you do not use.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution.
I mark the constraints: a 100 GiB gp2 volume, 8,000 IOPS needed, data that stays near 100 GiB, and minimal downtime.
Before I look at the options, I predict gp3, because gp3 provisions IOPS independently of volume size, and Elastic Volumes changes the type while the instance runs.

I remove the RAID 0 array, because it adds volumes and a move of the database files, which means more storage and downtime. I remove the larger gp2 volume, because gp2 gives 3 IOPS per GiB, so 8,000 IOPS needs many times the storage that the data uses.

Between gp3 and io2 Block Express the difference is what the higher price buys: higher durability, better latency consistency and more performance than gp3 gives; the stem asks for none of these, so gp3 is enough.
Check: gp3 with 8,000 IOPS keeps 100 GiB, changes in place and is the lowest cost SSD volume type. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: gp2 at 100 GiB gives only about 300 baseline IOPS. Modify the volume online to gp3 with Elastic Volumes and provision 8,000 IOPS at the same 100 GiB size; cheaper than growing gp2 or moving to io2.

items.stem: A company runs a media processing application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. Each instance writes many working files while it processes a job, and the job needs about 2,000 IOPS of small, random reads and writes on each instance. The company must make sure that the files are still there after the instances are stopped and started again for maintenance every weekend. Which storage solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: still there after the instances are stopped and started again
about 2,000 IOPS of small, random reads and writes

options.text: Launch the fleet on an instance type that provides instance store volumes, and write the working files to those volumes.
options.why: Instance store data is lost when the instance is [stopped, hibernated, or terminated](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop), so the weekend stop erases the files.

options.text: Attach a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
options.why: An EBS volume keeps its data through a stop, and gp3 includes a baseline of [3,000 IOPS](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-baseline-iops) in the price of storage, which covers this job.

options.text: Attach a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
options.why: It works, but io2 Block Express is for needs such as [consistent sub-millisecond latency](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases), while gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd).

options.text: Attach a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume to each instance, and write the working files to that volume.
options.why: Small, random I/O [won't perform well on HDD-backed volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-hdd-not-for-random-small-io), so a low price per GB does not help when the job needs fast I/O.

items.explanation: The deciding phrase is the weekend stop and start. An EBS volume is [off-instance storage](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-persists-independently-of-instance) that [remains attached throughout the stop-start cycle](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-stays-attached-through-stop-start), while instance store data is [cryptographically erased](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-data-persists-reboot-not-stop) at a stop. Among the EBS types, gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd), and its included [3,000 IOPS](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-baseline-iops) cover the 2,000 IOPS of each instance.
items.takeaway: Data that has to survive a stop goes on an EBS volume, not on instance store.
items.twin: If the stem said "the files are temporary scratch data that need the lowest latency" instead: instance store, because it gives [high random I/O performance with very low latency](../facts/instance-store.md#instance-store-ssd-high-random-io).

solvers.stem_only: The data must survive a stop and start, so instance store is out; EBS is needed. Small random I/O at about 2,000 IOPS fits General Purpose SSD (gp3), whose included baseline IOPS cover it at no extra charge; HDD types handle small random I/O poorly and io2 costs more than needed.

items.stem: A company stores financial records on Amazon EBS volumes in one AWS Region and takes a monthly snapshot of each volume. An auditor requires that each monthly snapshot is immutable for one year after the company creates it. Several administrators in the company's AWS account have full access to Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?
keywords: have full access to Amazon EC2

options.text: Lock each monthly snapshot in governance mode for one year, with the lock set as soon as the company creates the snapshot.
options.why: It locks the snapshots, but in governance mode [users with appropriate IAM permissions can unlock](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-governance-mode) them, so an administrator can still remove the protection.

options.text: Create a Recycle Bin retention rule that keeps deleted EBS snapshots for 365 days, and restore any snapshot that someone deletes.
options.why: Recycle Bin acts after a delete: a matching snapshot is [retained in the Recycle Bin](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-delete-retained-by-recycle-bin-rule), so users can still delete it, and it is not immutable.

options.text: Lock each monthly snapshot in compliance mode for one year, without a cooling-off period, as soon as the company creates the snapshot.
options.why: In compliance mode [you can't unlock the snapshot](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode) after the cooling-off period, and to delete it [you must wait for the lock to expire](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode).

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to every user and role that denies the ec2:DeleteSnapshot action on the monthly snapshots for one year.
options.why: Administrators with full access can edit or detach the policy and then delete a snapshot, while a locked snapshot is protected [regardless of their IAM permissions](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-no-user-can-delete).
options.misconception: believes that administrators cannot remove an IAM deny policy that applies to them

items.explanation: Immutable means that the snapshot stays for the whole year, whatever permissions an administrator has. In compliance mode, [you can't unlock the snapshot](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode) after the cooling-off period, and [you can only increase the lock duration](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode). Governance mode, an IAM policy and a Recycle Bin rule each leave an administrator a way to delete the snapshot.
items.takeaway: Immutable snapshots, safe from administrators too: lock them in compliance mode.
items.twin: If the stem said "a security team needs to remove a lock early after an approved review" instead: governance mode, because [users with appropriate IAM permissions can unlock](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-governance-mode) the snapshot.

solvers.stem_only: EBS Snapshot Lock in compliance mode for one year: nobody, including the root user and administrators, can delete the snapshot or shorten the lock once the cooling-off period (optional) has passed; governance mode and IAM denies can be undone by privileged admins.

items.stem: A company runs an application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The application keeps its data on an unencrypted Amazon EBS data volume. A new security policy requires the company to encrypt this data at rest. The company must also ensure that every new EBS volume that anyone creates in the Region from now on is encrypted. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a snapshot of the volume, copy the snapshot with encryption turned on, and replace the volume with a new volume from the copy.
options.why: [You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot), so you snapshot the volume and [create an encrypted copy of that snapshot](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot) for a new volume.

options.text: Use Elastic Volumes to modify the existing volume in place, and turn on encryption while the volume stays attached to the running instance of the application.
options.why: You [cannot change the encryption status](../facts/kms.md#kms-ebs-encryption-status-fixed-at-create) of an existing volume, so Elastic Volumes offers no setting that encrypts it in place.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in the Region, and wait for Amazon EBS to encrypt the existing volume in the background.
options.why: Encryption by default [has no effect on existing EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only), so the existing volume stays unencrypted.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in the Region, and keep the AWS managed key as the default encryption key.
options.why: Encryption by default is a [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region), and it ensures that [all new volumes are always encrypted](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) there.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that runs every hour, finds new unencrypted volumes in the Region, and replaces each one with an encrypted copy.
options.why: A scheduled function is code to build and run, and a new volume stays unencrypted until the next run; one [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) covers every new volume.
options.misconception: a custom scheduled job is needed to keep new volumes encrypted

items.explanation: Two needs decide this question: the existing data and every new volume. The existing data moves to an encrypted volume through an encrypted snapshot copy. Encryption by default then makes the account [enforce the encryption of the new EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only), with one Region setting and no code.
items.takeaway: Encrypt an existing volume through an encrypted snapshot copy; for new volumes, use the [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region).
items.twin: If the stem said "every new volume in two Regions" instead: turn on encryption by default in each Region, because it is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting).
items.say: The old volume goes through an encrypted snapshot copy, and encryption by default covers every new one.

solvers.stem_only: Enable EBS encryption by default in the Region for all new volumes; for the existing unencrypted volume, snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption (or create an encrypted volume from the snapshot), and swap volumes. Existing volumes cannot be encrypted in place.

items.stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in two AWS Regions, us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Teams in both Regions create new Amazon EBS volumes every day with their own scripts and templates. A new security policy requires that every new EBS volume in these two Regions is encrypted at rest. The company does not want to change the scripts and templates of the teams. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: every new EBS volume in these two Regions

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in us-east-1 only, because the setting then applies to every Region of the account.
options.why: Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting), so new volumes in eu-west-1 stay unencrypted.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in us-east-1 and in eu-west-1, and keep the AWS managed key of each Region as the default key.
options.why: Encryption by default is a [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) that ensures [all new volumes are always encrypted](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region), with no change to the scripts of the teams.

options.text: Run an AWS Lambda function every hour in each Region that finds unencrypted volumes and turns on encryption for each volume in place.
options.why: [You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot), so the function has no in-place step, and new volumes stay unencrypted between runs.

options.text: Create a customer managed key in each Region, turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in both Regions, and set each new key as the default key.
options.why: It works, but you then create and manage two keys, while EBS already has [a unique AWS managed key in each Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-aws-managed-key-alias-per-region).
options.misconception: encryption by default needs a customer managed key

items.explanation: Two Regions and the least effort decide this question. Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting), so you turn it on in each of the two Regions. After that, the account will [enforce the encryption of the new EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only) that the teams create there, and their scripts stay the same.
items.takeaway: Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting): turn it on in every Region where teams create volumes.
items.twin: If the stem said "the existing volumes must also be encrypted" instead: also replace each one from an encrypted snapshot copy, because encryption by default [has no effect on existing EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only).
items.say: Encryption by default is per Region, so I'd turn it on in both Regions.

solvers.stem_only: EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting: turn it on in both Regions; the AWS managed key (aws/ebs) is enough since no key control is required.

items.stem: A company must keep one Amazon EBS snapshot of a database volume for each month for seven years to meet a compliance rule. The snapshots are kept for long-term storage and are infrequently accessed. When an audit needs an old snapshot, a restore that takes up to three days is acceptable. The company currently keeps all of these monthly snapshots in the standard tier. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to keep these snapshots?
keywords: a restore that takes up to three days is acceptable

options.text: Keep the monthly snapshots in the standard tier, and add a tag to each snapshot that marks it as part of the compliance record.
options.why: It meets the rule, but the archive tier offers [up to 75 percent lower snapshot storage costs](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-75-percent-lower-cost) for rarely accessed snapshots.
options.misconception: the standard tier is the only place to keep an EBS snapshot

options.text: Copy the monthly snapshots into an Amazon S3 bucket through the Amazon S3 API, and store them in the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.
options.why: EBS snapshots are [only available through the Amazon EC2 API](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-snapshots-not-via-s3-api), so the S3 API cannot copy them into a bucket.

options.text: Move each monthly snapshot to the Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive tier after it is created, and restore it from there for an audit.
options.why: AWS recommends the archive tier for [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily) that you keep for a long time and rarely restore.

options.text: Delete every monthly snapshot except the most recent one, because the newest snapshot holds all of the data that the volume needs.
options.why: The newest snapshot restores the volume as it is today, and the compliance rule needs the state of each month.
options.misconception: the latest snapshot holds every earlier state of the volume

items.explanation: Seven years of monthly snapshots that are rarely restored decide this question. AWS recommends the archive tier for [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily), and its storage costs less than the standard tier. A restore from the archive tier can take [up to 72 hours](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours), which the three-day limit allows.
items.takeaway: Monthly snapshots kept for years and rarely restored belong in the EBS Snapshots Archive tier.
items.twin: If the stem said "an auditor needs a snapshot within one hour" instead: keep the snapshots in the standard tier, because an archive restore can take [up to 72 hours](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours).
items.say: Monthly snapshots kept for years go to the archive tier.

solvers.stem_only: Move the monthly snapshots to EBS Snapshots Archive: full snapshots kept at much lower storage cost for long retention, restore takes up to 72 hours, minimum 90-day retention fits seven years.

items.stem: A company runs a database on one Amazon EC2 instance that stores its data on one Amazon EBS volume. The company accepts the loss of up to one day of data and a recovery time of several hours. The company does not run any of its instances across multiple Availability Zones today. The company must be able to recover the database if the whole Region becomes unavailable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: if the whole Region becomes unavailable
loss of up to one day of data

options.text: Take a daily snapshot of the volume. After a failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone of the same Region.
options.why: A restore in another zone stays in the same Region, because [snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing), and that whole Region is down.

options.text: Take a daily snapshot of the volume and copy it to a second Region. After a failure, create a volume from the copy there.
options.why: You can [copy snapshots from one Region to another](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt), so a daily copy in a second Region restores the database there within the one-day loss limit.

options.text: Keep the data on the current volume. After a failure, detach the volume and attach it to a new instance in another Availability Zone of the Region.
options.why: The volume and the instance [must be in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance), and the whole Region is down, so the volume cannot be attached anywhere.

options.text: Take a daily snapshot and copy it to a second Region. Keep a standby instance running there, and restore each new copy to its volume.
options.why: It works, but a standby instance that runs every day costs more than a restore after a failure, and several hours of recovery are acceptable.
options.misconception: a database can be recovered only from a standby instance that is already running

items.explanation: The loss of the whole Region, with one day of data loss allowed, decides this question. [Snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing) where they are created, so a backup that must outlive the Region needs a copy in a second Region. You can [copy snapshots from one Region to another](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt) each day and restore the latest copy after a failure.
items.takeaway: A backup that has to outlive a Region needs a snapshot copy in a second Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable" instead: restore the latest snapshot in another zone, because you can [restore volumes in any Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region) of the Region.
items.say: If the whole Region can fail, the snapshot needs a copy in a second Region.

solvers.stem_only: Daily snapshots copied to a second Region (cross-Region snapshot copy, e.g. via Data Lifecycle Manager); after a Regional failure, create a volume from the copy and launch an instance there. No running standby needed for an RTO of hours.
